text:
Case study: Kabyaza (Kabyaza, Rwanda)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** This case study encompasses two distinct but related sub-cases of managed community resettlement in Rwanda, both embedded within Rwanda's national villagization and Integrated Development Programme (IDP) policy framework:

- **Sub-case A:** Nyabihu/Musanze Model Green Village Resettlement — Nyabihu and Musanze Districts, Northwestern Province, Rwanda (primary documentation: Kabyaza Green Village)
- **Sub-case B:** Rweru Model Green Village (RMGV) — Bugesera District, Eastern Province, Rwanda (resettlement from Mazane and Sharita Islands)

The two sub-cases are distinct in geography, hazard profile, and evidence base, but both sit within Rwanda's broader villagization and rural settlement policy context. They are treated jointly in this memo because both appear in the reviewed source documents as examples of Rwanda's nationally coordinated managed resettlement approach.

**Hazards:**
- *Nyabihu/Musanze:* Recurrent flooding, soil erosion, and landslides on steep hillside terrain; drought and erratic rainfall affecting agricultural productivity (Adaptation Fund, 2019).
- *Rweru/Bugesera:* Flooding from the Nyabarongo River overflowing its banks; inundation risk for island communities; limited access to services compounding hazard vulnerability (Dale & Ajibade, 2025). The Eastern Province is less prone to landslides than northwestern Rwanda, but Bugesera District faces the highest flood risk within the province (Dale & Ajibade, 2025).

**Type of Retreat:** State-led, planned community resettlement into purpose-built "Model Green Villages" (imidugudu). This is not a market-based property buyout programme. The government provided new housing in exchange for departure from high-risk origin sites, constructing climate-resilient homes, and delivering social services infrastructure in the receiving villages.

**Scale:**
- *Nyabihu/Musanze (Adaptation Fund project):* 200 extremely poor households resettled to Kabyaza Green Village (Adaptation Fund, 2019). Separately, a New Times report (December 2016) reported 455 vulnerable families received new homes across the broader Nyabihu district resettlement programme — a wider figure that extends beyond the Kabyaza component alone.
- *Rweru:* Prior to relocation, an estimated 2,000 people lived on Mazane and Sharita Islands. At the time of June 2021 fieldwork, 1,777 individuals in 296 households were living in RMGV; an additional 331 households from Sharita remained to be relocated (Dale & Ajibade, 2025). The RMGV was resettled in four phases between 2016 and 2020.
- *National context:* Dale & Ajibade (2025), citing The New Times (2012), report that the IDP had resettled an estimated 61,890 families nationwide since 2017 — a contextual background figure rather than a case-specific result.

**Key Actors:**
- *Nyabihu/Musanze sub-case:* Rwanda Ministry of Environment (national implementing entity for the Adaptation Fund project); Rwanda Water and Forest Authority (executing entity); Adaptation Fund (US$9.97 million Direct Access grant); UNDP and UNEP (co-implementing partners). District authorities managed local implementation. (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- *Rweru sub-case:* The Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) constructed housing; key informant interviews in Dale & Ajibade (2025) included representatives from the Rwandan Housing Authority, REMA, MINAGRI, MINALOC, Bugesera District leadership, and the Rweru Sector administration. These actors operated within the broader IDP policy framework rather than as co-implementers of a single joint project structure.
- Across both sub-cases, the Government of Rwanda is the central directing actor.
- Academics from Columbia University and Emory University (Dale & Ajibade) conducted post-resettlement fieldwork.

**Timeline:**
- Rwanda's Human Settlement Policy (imidugudu) established: 1996 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- Rural Settlement Programme adopted: 2008 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- Pilot model green villages established (Rubaya and Muyebe): 2011 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- National Land Use and Development Master Plan adopted: 2011 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- Rwanda Ministry of Environment accredited as Adaptation Fund national implementing entity: 2011 (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- Adaptation Fund project (Nyabihu/Musanze) begins: 2014; concludes: 2019; grant: US$9.97 million (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- RMGV inaugurated; first resettlement phase begins: 2016 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- New Times reports 455 Nyabihu families received new homes: December 2016 (NewTimes, 2016)
- Green Climate Fund scale-up project approved (informed by Adaptation Fund experience): 2018 (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- RMGV phased resettlement completed (four phases): 2016–2020 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- Dale & Ajibade fieldwork conducted at RMGV: May–June 2021 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)

**Key Outcomes:**
*Positive:* Construction of climate-resilient housing; improved access to health care, schools, markets, and transportation for remote island communities; reduced physical exposure to flooding; adoption of some climate-resilient farming practices in Nyabihu; 178 cows distributed cooperatively to Rweru households; the Adaptation Fund project is described as informing a GCF scale-up and replication of activities nationally (Adaptation Fund, 2019; Dale & Ajibade, 2025). The project describes women-headed households as empowered, with more than half of Kabyaza households female-headed (Adaptation Fund, 2019).

*Negative and unresolved:* Smaller and less fertile agricultural plots in Rweru; food insecurity and reduced crop productivity; approximately 42% of Rweru residents reported receiving no compensation for island property losses; land titles had not been provided to resettled households at the time of 2021 fieldwork; restrictions on keeping livestock other than cows; intra-community inequity between resettlement phases; limited financial capital; access to drinking water remained difficult in RMGV; COVID-19 pandemic erased some early livelihood gains (Dale & Ajibade, 2025).

**Narrative Summary:**

Rwanda has pursued one of Sub-Saharan Africa's most systematically embedded rural resettlement programmes, rooted in its post-genocide villagization policy and increasingly framed as climate change adaptation. The programme clusters dispersed rural households into planned settlements (imidugudu) to improve access to services, reduce hazard exposure, and support poverty reduction. Two cases illustrate this approach in different geographic and hazard contexts. In Nyabihu and Musanze Districts of Northwestern Province, the Adaptation Fund supported the resettlement of 200 highly vulnerable households from flood-prone and landslide-prone hillside areas into the Kabyaza Green Village, where climate-resilient homes with biogas systems and rainwater harvesting were built and livelihoods support was provided. Separately, in Bugesera District's Eastern Province, approximately 2,000 people from two remote islands (Mazane and Sharita) on a lake system near the Burundi border were relocated in four phases between 2016 and 2020 to the Rweru Model Green Village — a purpose-built settlement with schools, a health centre, and shared cowsheds. Dale & Ajibade (2025) caution that the Rweru case should be understood as embedded in Rwanda's broader regional development and villagization strategy rather than as a purely climate-based relocation.

Both relocations illustrate the double-edged nature of state-led transformative resettlement. For Rweru residents, the move brought meaningful gains: safer housing, access to health care, schools, markets, and transportation — services entirely absent on the islands, where residents faced two-hour canoe journeys and drew unfiltered drinking water from the lake. Yet the resettlement also imposed serious constraints. Agricultural plots in Rweru are smaller and less fertile than island lands; the shift from island ecosystems to a drier mainland microclimate created food insecurity; and about 42% of residents reported receiving no compensation for property losses. Residents had not received land titles at the time of fieldwork in 2021, limiting access to credit. Intra-community inequities between resettlement phases — some early arrivals received furniture while later arrivals did not — generated resentment. COVID-19 compounded these difficulties by closing markets and disrupting livelihoods (Dale & Ajibade, 2025).

The voluntariness of the move is complex. While 76% of Rweru respondents said they moved because the government mandated it, 39% said residents had been requesting the move for years. The Mazane Island population faced a fully mandatory relocation — Mazane was subsequently converted to military use, and return is prohibited — while Sharita residents retained some access to former croplands. The programme was government-directed, with community consultation limited largely to informing residents of the pending move. The Adaptation Fund (2019) describes residents as "involved in the project's decision-making processes," primarily through the "muganda" monthly maintenance assemblies rather than co-design of the resettlement itself. Authors Dale & Ajibade (2025) report that many government experts and practitioners in Rwanda explained that the full range of benefits from resettlement would not be fully realized for at least another generation, as children in the new villages gain education and skills. The case offers important lessons — both positive and cautionary — for planned resettlement as climate adaptation in the Global South.

text:
Case study: Kabyaza (Kabyaza, Rwanda)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Direct answer:** Primarily **Proactive**, with reactive contextual elements.

**Narrative:** The resettlement in both Nyabihu/Musanze and Rweru was not triggered by a single acute disaster event. Rather, it was embedded within Rwanda's long-standing national villagization policy (imidugudu, 1996) and the Rural Settlement Programme (2008), which proactively identified high-risk zones and planned settlements in advance. Dale & Ajibade (2025, p. 27) note that the Government of Rwanda's prioritization of resettlement from "steep slopes above a 20% grade" was based on ex-ante risk identification facilitated by GIS terrain mapping through the National Land Use and Development Master Plan (adopted 2011). The Adaptation Fund project (2014–2019) was planned in advance to reduce vulnerability to recurring floods, landslides, and erosion in Nyabihu/Musanze (Adaptation Fund, 2019). The Rweru resettlement similarly involved advance planning: island communities were informed of the pending move, and resettlement occurred in four planned phases between 2016 and 2020 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025).

Reactive contextual elements are present: the resettlement responded to well-established and ongoing hazard impacts. The Mugogo lowlands downstream of the Kinoni River "had even become a lake due to persistent floods, leaving farmers awash without land to cultivate" by the time the Adaptation Fund project began (Adaptation Fund, 2019, p. 1). In Rweru, 76% of respondents described their lives before relocation as dangerous, citing flooding and island inundation as primary risks (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 30). These ongoing hazard conditions informed the urgency of the programme but were not a single post-disaster trigger.

**Coding rationale:** "Proactive" is the primary code because resettlement was institutionally planned in advance of further disaster occurrence, anchored in national risk-reduction policy rather than in response to a specific event. Reactive elements are present as contextual background — the programme addressed accumulated and ongoing hazard damage — but proactive planning was the dominant mode.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Date:**
- Adaptation Fund project (Nyabihu/Musanze): began 2014, concluded 2019 (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- Rwanda Ministry of Environment accredited as Adaptation Fund implementing entity: 2011 (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- Kabyaza Green Village / Nyabihu broader programme: 455 families reported as having received new homes by December 2016 (NewTimes, 2016)
- RMGV inaugurated: 2016; phased resettlement 2016–2020; Dale & Ajibade fieldwork: June 2021 (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)
- GCF scale-up project approved: 2018 (Adaptation Fund, 2019)

**Number of households affected:**
- *Nyabihu/Musanze — Kabyaza Green Village component:* 200 extremely poor households resettled (Adaptation Fund, 2019, p. 2)
- *Nyabihu district broader programme:* 455 vulnerable families reported to have received new homes (NewTimes, 2016) — this is a wider figure than the Kabyaza component alone
- *Rweru (RMGV):* 1,777 individuals in 296 households resident at time of June 2021 fieldwork; an additional 331 households from Sharita remained to be relocated (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28)
- Prior to relocation, an estimated 2,000 people lived on Mazane and Sharita Islands (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)

**Number of population affected:**
- *Nyabihu/Musanze:* 21,429 people (50% women) from target households reported to have a new source of income through the Adaptation Fund project (Adaptation Fund, 2019, p. 2) — this encompasses the broader project beneficiaries, not only resettled households
- *Rweru:* approximately 2,000 people originally on islands; 1,777 individuals in RMGV at time of 2021 fieldwork (Dale & Ajibade, 2025)

**Total funding:**
- US$9.97 million from the Adaptation Fund (Direct Access grant) for the Nyabihu/Musanze project (Adaptation Fund, 2019). The document also references this as a "US$10 million project" (p. 1); US$9.97 million is the precise grant amount.
- GCF scale-up approved 2018, informed by Adaptation Fund experience; amount not specified in reviewed sources (Adaptation Fund, 2019)
- UNDP and UNEP identified as co-implementing partners; no separate financial figures provided in reviewed sources
- Rweru sub-case: no separate project funding amount documented in reviewed sources

**Note on figures:** The 455-family figure (NewTimes, 2016) and the 200-household figure (Adaptation Fund, 2019) refer to different scope: the former is the broader Nyabihu district programme; the latter is specifically the Kabyaza Green Village component of the Adaptation Fund project. These should not be conflated. The 21,429 population figure includes all beneficiaries of the broader Adaptation Fund project activities (terracing, livelihood support, etc.), not only resettled households.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Direct answer:** **Multiple Hazards**

**Narrative:** Both sub-cases involve multiple co-occurring hazards. The Adaptation Fund (2019, p. 1) references "extreme rainfall, flooding, erosion and landslides, as well as drought" as the hazards affecting communities in Nyabihu/Musanze. Dale & Ajibade (2025, p. 25) identify "intense and frequent floods, landslides and droughts" as the hazards driving resettlement in Rwanda more broadly. In Nyabihu/Musanze, flooding, soil erosion, and landslides on steep slopes are the primary hazards. In Rweru/Bugesera, flooding from the Nyabarongo River is primary; the Eastern Province is less prone to landslides than northwestern Rwanda but Bugesera District faces high flood risk (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28). Drought and erratic rainfall are identified as additional stressors affecting agricultural productivity in both contexts.

**Coding rationale:** Multiple hazards clearly applies. The hazards are not purely cascading from a single initiating event but represent distinct and recurring threats operating concurrently or at different times.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Direct answer:** **Natural Hazard**

**Narrative:** All hazards identified in the reviewed sources are natural in origin: flooding, landslides, soil erosion, and drought. There is no evidence of technological or industrial hazard drivers in either sub-case. Dale & Ajibade (2025) note that Rwanda was ranked the 8th most climate-change-impacted country out of 196 in 2018, and the Adaptation Fund project is explicitly framed as a climate change adaptation initiative. However, per the codebook, the climate change category is noted as discarded from main analysis; "Natural Hazard" is therefore the applicable code. Climate change is noted as a significant contextual driver of hazard intensity and frequency but is not itself a codebook category.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Coastal Flooding/Erosion), (Riverine/Pluvial Flooding), (Lake Flooding/Erosion), (Wildfire), (Volcano), (Land Subsidence), (Landslide/Debris Flow), (Earthquake), (Tsunami), (Hurricane), (Other)

**Direct answer:**

- **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding: Yes** — Primary hazard. In Nyabihu/Musanze: flooding from the Kinoni River caused the Mugogo lowlands to become "a lake due to persistent floods" (Adaptation Fund, 2019, p. 1). In Rweru/Bugesera: flooding from the Nyabarongo River overflowing its banks is identified as the primary flood risk (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28).
- **Landslide/Debris Flow: Yes** — Primary hazard in Nyabihu/Musanze. Steep hillside terrain with slopes above a 20% grade places communities at persistent risk of landslides; this risk zone identification informed resettlement targeting (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 27; Adaptation Fund, 2019, p. 1).
- **Lake Flooding/Erosion: Possible/Uncertain** — Mazane and Sharita Islands were located on a lake/reservoir system near the Burundi border. Inundation and flooding risk from lake levels is implied but not explicitly described in the reviewed sources as "lake flooding" in a defined sense. This code is tentative.
- **Other (Drought/Erratic Rainfall): Yes** — Drought and erratic rainfall are identified as co-occurring stressors affecting rural livelihoods and agricultural productivity (Adaptation Fund, 2019, p. 1; Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 26). Soil erosion is an associated consequence of steep-slope farming rather than a separate hazard type per codebook definitions.
- **Coastal Flooding/Erosion: No** — Rwanda is landlocked.
- **Wildfire, Volcano, Land Subsidence, Earthquake, Tsunami, Hurricane: No evidence** in reviewed sources.

**Primary codes:** Riverine/Pluvial Flooding; Landslide/Debris Flow; Other (drought, erratic rainfall). Lake Flooding/Erosion: tentative/uncertain.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Direct answer:** **Entire Community** (Rweru/Mazane Island); **Neighbourhood/Groups** (Nyabihu, 200 households from scattered high-risk zones); **Sub-watershed** (watershed-scale land management interventions in Nyabihu/Musanze).

**Narrative:** The Rweru/RMGV resettlement involved the complete relocation of all residents of Mazane Island — nobody remained after relocation, and Mazane's prior total population was approximately 1,109 individuals (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28). This constitutes the relocation of an entire community. For Sharita, a substantial portion of residents were relocated (104 families, over 400 people at time of fieldwork), with 331 households remaining to be moved; some Sharita residents retained access to island croplands. In Nyabihu/Musanze, the Adaptation Fund project resettled 200 households from high-risk areas within the district to Kabyaza Green Village — these were households drawn from scattered high-risk zones rather than a geographically contiguous neighbourhood. The Adaptation Fund project also involved watershed-scale interventions (503 ha of bench terracing, drainage channel restoration, afforestation) across the Kinoni River catchment area (Adaptation Fund, 2019), operating at sub-watershed or watershed scale for land management purposes.

**Coding rationale:** "Entire community" applies to the Mazane Island case. "Neighbourhood" or "Groups" is the closer fit for the Nyabihu 200-household case, as households were drawn from scattered risk zones. "Sub-watershed" applies to the physical scope of land management activities in Nyabihu/Musanze, not to the resettlement scale per se.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Direct answer:** **Communities** (Mazane Island); **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (Sharita Island partial; Nyabihu 200 households from high-risk zones)

**Narrative:** The primary subjects of retreat are rural households, relocated collectively. The Adaptation Fund (2019, p. 2) describes resettling "200 extremely poor households from high-risk areas in Nyabihu District." Dale & Ajibade (2025) document the complete resettlement of Mazane Island's population and substantial resettlement of Sharita Island residents. In both cases, resettlement was collective rather than individual, targeting groups or whole communities. There is no evidence in reviewed sources of retreat of critical infrastructure, hazard protection structures, or industrial assets.

---

### Other notes (General Information)

The case study straddles two distinct geographic and institutional sub-cases with different hazard profiles, different institutional implementing arrangements, and different evidence bases. Sub-case A (Nyabihu/Musanze) is documented primarily by the Adaptation Fund (2019) project story with supplementary NewTimes reporting. Sub-case B (Rweru/Bugesera) is documented primarily by Dale & Ajibade (2025) through semi-structured interviews and key informant data. The national IDP policy framework connects both, but they should not be read as co-components of a single managed project. Dale & Ajibade (2025, p. 33) explicitly caution that the Rweru case should be "understood in the context of villagization as a regional and sustainable development strategy rather than a wholesale climate-based relocation." Coding responses below integrate evidence from both sub-cases and note which sub-case the evidence derives from where relevant.

---

text:
Case study: Kabyaza (Kabyaza, Rwanda)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Direct answer:** **Community buyout/retreat** (primary)

**Narrative:** The programme is fundamentally a community-level resettlement: entire communities or large groups were relocated collectively to purpose-built villages. This is not an individual buyout programme in the sense of market-based property acquisition from individual homeowners. No evidence of financial purchase of individual properties from households is found in reviewed sources. Instead, the government provided new housing in exchange for departure from high-risk areas. Mazane Island was subsequently converted to military use. Sharita residents retained some access to former croplands (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28–29). The mechanism is state-led in-kind provision of housing rather than financial compensation at market value.

**Coding rationale:** "Community buyout/retreat" is the closest applicable code, as relocation was collective and coordinated at the community level. "Individual buyout" does not apply — there was no financial purchase of individual properties. "Other acquisition tools" was considered but is not well-supported: there is no market buyout or formal financial acquisition mechanism documented. The mode is in-kind housing provision within a state-directed resettlement framework. No evidence of leasebacks, easements, or infrastructure realignment as primary mechanisms.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process? Are there any legal frameworks or regulations that guide the MR decision process?

**Direct answer:** **Relevant regulations/acts** (primary); **Retreat land development** (partial); **Title(s) transfer** (incomplete); **Land rezoning** (implied, for Mazane). Legal authority over retreat is exercised by the Government of Rwanda through national policy but the specific legal instruments are described in policy terms rather than formal property law terms in reviewed sources.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** Multiple policy and legal frameworks govern the programme. Rwanda's Human Settlement Policy (imidugudu, 1996), the Rural Settlement Programme (2008, Government of Rwanda, 2009 as cited in Dale & Ajibade, 2025), Vision 2020, the Economic Development and Poverty Reduction Strategy (EDPRS), the National Strategy for Transformation (GoR, 2017), and the National Land Use and Development Master Plan (2011) all frame and authorize resettlement (Dale & Ajibade, 2025). The Green Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy (GoR, 2011) embeds climate adaptation within national policy. The Ubudehe Programme provides a poverty-targeting framework. The IDP with its eleven pillars provides the operational framework.

- **Land acquisition:** Origin-site lands were effectively absorbed by the state in the case of Mazane Island, which was converted to military use (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28). Sharita residents retained some access to former croplands. There is no evidence in reviewed sources of formal legal property acquisition processes (e.g., compulsory purchase orders) or compensation paid for land.

- **Title(s) transfer (incomplete):** Resettled households had not received land titles to their new properties at the time of the 2021 fieldwork. "New residents had not been given land titles to their new properties at the time of this research, and without secure land tenure, access to credit had been difficult" (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 32).

- **Retreat land development:** The Kabyaza Green Village and RMGV were newly constructed according to government-specified green village templates (clay bricks, biogas systems, shared cowsheds, rainwater tanks) (Dale & Ajibade, 2025; Adaptation Fund, 2019). The Rwanda Defense Force constructed housing in Rweru (Dale & Ajibade, 2025, p. 28).

- **Land rezoning:** Mazane Island's conversion to military use implies a change in land use designation, though this is not formally described as a rezoning process in reviewed sources.

- **Compliance & enforcement:** The Rweru relocation was mandatory for island residents, and the conversion of Mazane to military use makes return impossible. Dale & Ajibade (2025, p. 28) note: "vis
